clue.text: Media mogul to a large extent makes case for regular use of radio

indicators.note: a case surrounds its contents, so these words put one piece around the other

parts.note: to a large extent means much, as in 'not much changed'

indicators.note: regular use means taking every other letter of the word radio, starting with the first

explanation.surface: A press baron largely owes his power to habitual use of the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regular use of' takes the first, third and fifth letters of 'radio', and 'makes case for' wraps the word for 'to a large extent' around them. 'Media mogul' points at the theme: the News International hacking scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert Murdoch is the Australian-born proprietor of a global newspaper and television empire.

clue.text: Dig up dirt on Sun, going topless? On the contrary

indicators.note: the clue sets dirt on, above, the paper; on the contrary means that order is turned about, so the paper's letters go to the front

parts.note: dirt means earth or soil

indicators.note: going topless means losing the top letter, here the first letter of the word sun

parts.note: the Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, written as the word itself

explanation.surface: A tabloid digs up scandal about its own topless models, or maybe the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going topless' removes the S of SUN; 'on' would set dirt above the paper in this down entry, and 'On the contrary' flips that order. The Sun is a British tabloid famous for topless models.
explanation.definitionFit: To unearth something is to excavate it from the ground, as a dog does a buried bone.

clue.text: Top cops taking care of equipment for playing recordings

parts.note: detective inspectors, senior police officers, are DIs
c/o, written CO, is the postal abbreviation for care of

explanation.surface: Senior police officers take custody of some confiscated audio gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A mobile disco is the turntables, speakers and lights a DJ brings to play music at a party.

clue.text: Morgan's welcome contracts with American who's fabulously rich

indicators.note: contracts means shrinks, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: Morgan is a typical Welsh name, and croeso is the Welsh word for welcome
US, short for United States, means American

explanation.surface: Piers Morgan greets and signs deals with a wealthy American.
explanation.walkthrough: Morgan seems to be the former Mirror editor Piers Morgan, but it stands for any Welsh person; 'contracts' trims CROESO to CROES. The definition reads as 'one who's fabulously rich'.
explanation.definitionFit: Croesus, king of ancient Lydia, was so wealthy that his name became a byword for a man of vast riches.

clue.text: Artist's phone hacked by horrible woman

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: the second piece breaks into the first, as a hacker gets inside a phone

parts.note: to phone someone is to call them
a hag is an ugly, unpleasant old woman

explanation.surface: A painter discovers that a nasty woman has been hacking his phone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hacked by' puts the woman inside the phone word, echoing the phone-hacking scandal. The 's after the definition is short for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Marc Chagall was a Russian-French modernist painter known for dreamy village scenes and floating figures.

clue.text: Braying chap's expression showing inquiry a hint of worry

parts.note: chap means a man, he
eh? is a short spoken inquiry asking someone to repeat themselves

indicators.note: a hint gives only a trace, here the first letter of the word worry

explanation.surface: A loud-mouthed man's face shows a query and a trace of anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a hint of' takes W from 'worry'. 'Braying' in the surface describes the chap, but it is the definition: the donkey's cry.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey's noisy call is written as a two-part imitation of its sound, so the cry and the braying are one.

clue.text: Monarch, embraced by ghastly mogul, requiring lithium for nerves?

indicators.note: being embraced means being held inside, so one piece goes within the other
ghastly signals that the letters of mogul are in a horrible mess and must be rearranged

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the royal cipher of the Queen
Li is the chemical symbol for lithium

explanation.surface: The Queen is hugged by an awful media tycoon who needs lithium to calm himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ghastly' rearranges the letters of 'mogul' and 'embraced by' sets the Queen's cipher inside them. Lithium is a drug for mood disorders, which makes 'nerves' read as anxiety; the question mark flags the anatomical stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Glomeruli are tiny knots of vessels or nerve fibres, such as the clusters in the olfactory bulb, so the query marks a loose sense.

clue.text: Warning signs of end to scandal sheet on Sunday

indicators.note: the end of the word scandal is its final letter

parts.note: a plate is a thin flat sheet of metal

explanation.surface: The tail end of a tabloid exposé published at the weekend serves as a warning.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain L-plates are red L-on-white signs on a car driven by a learner, warning other road users.
explanation.definitionFit: Learner drivers must display these placards so others know to take care around them.

clue.text: Neutering a sinister lot, originally infiltrated by Independent

indicators.note: one piece slips inside the other, as an agent infiltrates a group
originally here means in an original, novel way, so the letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: Castrating a shady gang that this newspaper has infiltrated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' asks for A SINISTER LOT made new, and 'infiltrated by' slips the I for Independent into that rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterilisation removes the ability to breed, which is what neutering an animal achieves.

clue.text: We'd no self-worth, working here?

indicators.note: working means in operation, so the letters of the first words are set to work in a new order

explanation.surface: Staff at a disgraced tabloid confess they felt worthless working there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges the fourteen letters of WE'D NO SELF-WORTH. The whole clue then describes the paper, which closed in 2011 over phone hacking.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sunday tabloid shut down amid the hacking scandal, a place whose staff might well feel ashamed.

clue.text: See 10
Former editor's scam shrouded in deceptive humbug

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: a shroud wraps around, so the second piece is wrapped round the first

parts.note: BS, short for bullshit, is deceptive nonsense or humbug
to rook someone is to swindle or scam them

explanation.surface: A former tabloid editor's fraud is cloaked in misleading nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shrouded in' wraps the humbug letters round the scam. Rebekah Brooks edited the News of the World and The Sun and was charged over phone hacking.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebekah Brooks had edited Murdoch's News of the World and Sun before becoming chief executive of his British papers.

clue.text: Bent sergeant finding chemical substances

indicators.note: bent means twisted out of shape, so the letters of sergeant are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A corrupt police sergeant is found with illegal chemicals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' is British slang for corrupt, which suits a police sergeant, but here it rearranges SERGEANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Reagents are compounds used in a laboratory to bring about or detect a reaction.

clue.text: Extensive and unedited reporting of spanker?

parts.note: an unedited text is complete, whole

indicators.note: reporting means telling out loud, so the next word's sound is what counts

parts.note: a spanker is a fore-and-aft sail on the aftermost mast of a ship

explanation.surface: A full, uncut account of a man who smacks people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reporting of' gives a word that sounds like SAIL; a spanker looks like a person who spanks, but it is a ship's sail.
explanation.definitionFit: Wholesale changes are sweeping and comprehensive rather than limited.

clue.text: Complicated network's listening equipment

definitions.meaning: a complicated network of paths or passages is a maze
the inner ear, the bony cavity that holds the hearing organ, is called by this name

explanation.surface: An intricate web of connections that includes bugging devices.
explanation.definitionFit: A maze is a tangle of paths, and anatomists give the same name to the convoluted cavity of the inner ear.

clue.text: Copper starts to realise some editors are evil

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: the starts are the first letters of the words realise, some and editors

explanation.surface: A policeman begins to grasp that some newspaper editors are wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a police officer, but it is the metal; 'starts to' takes R, S and E.
explanation.definitionFit: A curse is a bane or affliction, something harmful that blights a life.

clue.text: Press at first wrongly take heart from Leveson Inquiry

indicators.note: at first means the opening letter of the word press

parts.note: to rob is to take something wrongly from someone

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, here the middle of Leveson

explanation.surface: The press initially lost heart through the Leveson Inquiry into its ethics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' gives P, 'heart from' the central E of LEVESON. The Leveson Inquiry (2011-12) examined British press ethics after phone hacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A probe is an investigation, especially an official one into wrongdoing.

clue.text: Investigative journalist for The Thunderer?

definitions.meaning: one who rumbles, finds out or exposes, a deception
something that rumbles like thunder; The Thunderer is also the nickname of The Times newspaper

explanation.surface: A Times reporter who digs up secrets.
explanation.walkthrough: The Thunderer is the old nickname of The Times, which tempts a solver toward a newspaper; the question mark points to something that literally rumbles.
explanation.definitionFit: To rumble a scheme is British slang for exposing it, and thunder rumbles, so one word fits both a sleuth and a noisy storm.

clue.text: Link second of hacking cases to nasty individual going undercover

indicators.note: going undercover means slipping inside, so one piece is hidden within the other
the second letter of the word hacking
nasty signals a nasty mess, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: I, the Roman numeral one, stands for an individual

explanation.surface: An associate in hacking cases, a nasty man who goes undercover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second of' takes the second letter of 'hacking'; 'nasty' rearranges it with the next two words to make ASSOCATE; 'going undercover' sends the individual inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To associate two things is to connect them in the mind, to join one idea with another.

clue.text: Old Bill, ignoring problem, end up taking line that's more than stupid

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving something out, so the problem is dropped from the word bill

parts.note: bill written as the word itself
a problem or ailment is an ill

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top
taking away the line means it is removed from the word for end

parts.note: an end, the outcome of something, is a result

explanation.surface: The police, ignoring a difficulty, end up following a line of thinking that's beyond dim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Bill' looks like British slang for the police, but splits in two; 'ignoring' drops the problem from the second word; 'taking' removes the line from the end word to make RESUT, which 'up' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone obtuse is slow-witted, so this comparative means even duller, beyond merely stupid.

clue.text: Support what David Sullivan managed to do, according to Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner, the Oxford don famed for swapping the opening sounds of words, signals that switch here

parts.words: what David Sullivan managed to do
parts.note: David Sullivan, the porn and Sunday Sport tycoon, bought a football team, co-owning Birmingham City and later West Ham

parts.words: what David Sullivan managed to do
parts.note: the second word of the phrase buy team

explanation.surface: Backing for whatever the newspaper and football tycoon pulled off, in a Spoonerism.
explanation.walkthrough: BUY TEAM with its opening sounds swapped becomes TIE BEAM. David Sullivan published the Sunday Sport tabloid and bought West Ham United.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie beam is a horizontal timber joining the feet of rafters, a structural support in a roof.

clue.text: Account involving married footballer and me appearing in The Mirror

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married in genealogies and forms

indicators.note: a mirror shows things back to front, so the words before are turned round

parts.note: Rio Ferdinand, the England defender, is a footballer known by his first name
me written as the word itself

explanation.surface: A married footballer's story told about me in the Daily Mirror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appearing in The Mirror' turns the footballer and 'me' back to front as one run, giving EMOIR. The Mirror is a British tabloid, which hides the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: A memoir is a written account of the author's own life and experiences.

clue.text: Abrupt, abrasive, low-down journalist finally achieving prominence

indicators.note: abrupt means cut short, so the following word loses its last letter

parts.note: emery is a gritty abrasive used on nail files and sandpaper
gen is British slang for information, the low-down

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of the word journalist

explanation.surface: A curt, harsh, sleazy reporter eventually rises to fame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abrupt' trims EMERY to EMER and 'finally' takes T from 'journalist'; 'abrasive' reads as a manner but is a substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Something emergent is coming into view or rising to notice.

clue.text: London's police subject to oversight at last!

parts.note: a theme is the subject of a talk or piece of writing

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of the word oversight

explanation.surface: Metropolitan officers finally made answerable to independent scrutiny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at last' gives T. The Met is short for the Metropolitan Police, criticised over its handling of the hacking inquiry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Metropolitan Police Service, known by a short nickname, is the force covering Greater London.

clue.text: Ogling parts of fey ingenue

indicators.note: the answer is made up of parts of these words, running from one into the next

explanation.surface: Staring lecherously at bits of a whimsical young actress.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogling is looking at someone with obvious desire, a form of staring closely.

clue.text: Coulson rag, all about banging

indicators.note: all about signals the letters are scattered around and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tabloid edited by Andy Coulson, all about sex.
explanation.walkthrough: Andy Coulson was editor of the News of the World and later jailed over phone hacking; 'rag' is slang for a tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: Clangorous describes a loud ringing, clanging din, like metal being struck.

clue.text: Story involving sex seems to occur regularly

parts.note: it is a coy euphemism for sex, as in doing it

indicators.note: occurring regularly means taking every other letter of the word seems, starting with the second

explanation.surface: A tabloid tale about sex seems to crop up all the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to occur regularly' takes E and M from 'seems'.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is a single piece of news in a paper or bulletin.

clue.text: They're seeking to get rid of top elements in media family

indicators.note: the top elements are the opening letters, here the first two, which are thrown away

parts.note: people who are seeking something are searchers

explanation.surface: Investigators set out to oust the senior members of a newspaper dynasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get rid of top elements' drops SE. The Archers is a long-running BBC radio soap about a farming family.
explanation.definitionFit: The Archers are the fictional farming clan at the heart of Britain's longest-running radio drama.

clue.text: One's getting a cheque, having turned round folding paper

indicators.note: turned round means the whole string of words before it reads backwards

parts.note: one's means one is, which is I'm, written IM
a giro is a British cheque for a state benefit payment

explanation.surface: A man gets a welfare payment after a change of heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having turned round' reverses the whole run of pieces at once. A giro was the cheque in which British unemployment benefit was paid.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into decorative shapes.
